scenes.heading: What RPA is and where it fits
scenes.caption: “What RPA is and where it fits” is a beginner lecture in RPA with UiPath, on the day about Automation foundations. Nothing in it is skipped. The scenes walk What RPA is and where it fits, each with a plain explanation and a small example.

scenes.heading: Why this lecture exists
scenes.caption: An RPA (Robotic Process Automation) developer builds software bots that automate repetitive, rule-based work such as data entry, invoice processing and report generation. This hour, “What RPA is and where it fits”, is where that becomes concrete. If you skip it, later talk about Automation foundations turns into words you cannot cash.

items: RPA with UiPath, beginner level
Today’s theme: Automation foundations
Separate ideas in this hour: What RPA is and where it fits

scenes.heading: The other hours today
scenes.caption: The rest of today is RPA vs traditional automation and AI, Attended vs unattended bots, and RPA tools and the certification path. Those are separate lectures with their own scenes. You will not be taught them here, and this lecture will not be repeated there. Learn What RPA is and where it fits now, well enough that those later hours can use the words.

items: RPA vs traditional automation and AI
Attended vs unattended bots
RPA tools and the certification path

scenes.heading: What RPA is
scenes.caption: The question in this scene is “What RPA is”. Answer it in ordinary words before you reach for a formal definition. In RPA with UiPath, a useful answer names the problem it solves and one place you would meet it while using UiPath Studio.

scenes.heading: Example: What RPA is

scenes.heading: Variables
scenes.caption: Variables are names for values. Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment. Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable.

items: Variables are names for values
Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment
Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable

scenes.heading: Step by step: Variables
scenes.caption: Give each value a name that says what it is for. Read a name to get the current value. Assign a new value when the fact changes. Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

items: Give each value a name that says what it is for.
Read a name to get the current value.
Assign a new value when the fact changes.
Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

items: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Two names can point at the same list or object. Changing one can change the other.

items: Two names can point at the same list or object. Changing one can change the other.

scenes.heading: scope
scenes.caption: Scope is the region of the program where a name can be seen. A name created inside a function is usually invisible outside it. Scope is why two functions can both use a variable called count and not smash each other.

items: Scope is the region of the program where a name can be seen
A name created inside a function is usually invisible outside it
Scope is why two functions can both use a variable called count and not smash each other

scenes.heading: Step by step: scope
scenes.caption: Notice where the name is created. Inside that block, the name is visible. Outside that block, it is not, unless you passed it or returned it. When two names match, the nearest enclosing one wins.

items: Notice where the name is created.
Inside that block, the name is visible.
Outside that block, it is not, unless you passed it or returned it.
When two names match, the nearest enclosing one wins.

scenes.heading: Detail: scope
scenes.caption: A loop variable is often scoped to the loop. Using it after the loop is a common bug in some languages and a design smell in all of them.

items: A loop variable is often scoped to the loop. Using it after the loop is a common bug in some languages and a design smell in all of them.

scenes.caption: Here is a small example of scope. Read each line and say what it changes. function f() { let n = 1 } n is not available after f returns. If you need it outside, return it. If you can change one piece and predict the new result, you have it.

lines: function f() { let n = 1 }
n is not available after f returns.
If you need it outside, return it.

scenes.heading: virtual environments
scenes.caption: A virtual environment is a private folder of Python packages for one project. Installing a library there does not change the Python other projects use. Without one, two projects fight over versions of the same library, and you cannot reproduce the setup.

scenes.heading: files
scenes.caption: A file is named data on disk. A program can read it, write it, and must close it, including when an error happens halfway. Paths are part of the problem. A relative path depends on the folder you ran the program from, which may not be the folder you expected.

scenes.heading: Logging
scenes.caption: Logging is writing a record of what the program did, so you can reconstruct a failure later. A useful log names the request, the decision, and the error. A useless log is either silent or a firehose of noise nobody reads.

items: Logging is writing a record of what the program did, so you can reconstruct a failure later

scenes.heading: Step by step: Logging
scenes.caption: Log at the boundary: request in, error, important decision. Include an id that ties lines from one request together. Do not log secrets, passwords, or full card numbers. Use levels. Debug is not an alert.

scenes.caption: Debugging is the disciplined search for why the program does something other than what you intended. You form a hypothesis, you check it, you change one thing. Guessing randomly feels faster and is slower. A hypothesis you can test beats staring.

scenes.heading: Variables
scenes.caption: Variables are names for values. Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment. Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable.

items: Variables are names for values
Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment
Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable

scenes.heading: Step by step: Variables
scenes.caption: Give each value a name that says what it is for. Read a name to get the current value. Assign a new value when the fact changes. Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

items: Give each value a name that says what it is for.
Read a name to get the current value.
Assign a new value when the fact changes.
Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

items: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Two names can point at the same list or object. Changing one can change the other.

items: Two names can point at the same list or object. Changing one can change the other.

scenes.heading: Example: Variables
scenes.caption: Here is a small example of Variables. Read each line and say what it changes. lives = 3 lives = lives - 1 The name lives now means 2. If you can change one piece and predict the new result, you have it.

lives = lives - 1
The name lives now means 2.

scenes.caption: Git is a tool that remembers every saved version of your project. A commit is one saved snapshot with a message about why it exists. It is how teams work on the same code without overwriting each other, and how you undo a change that looked fine yesterday.

scenes.caption: Define a few signals that mean “a user is hurt”. Alert on those, not on every wiggle. Look at the signal when you deploy. Write down what normal looks like so a graph means something.

scenes.heading: Building an RPA portfolio
scenes.caption: “Building an RPA portfolio” is an expert lecture in RPA with UiPath, on the day about Professional RPA development. Nothing in it is skipped. The scenes walk Building an RPA portfolio, each with a plain explanation and a small example.

scenes.heading: Why this lecture exists
scenes.caption: An RPA (Robotic Process Automation) developer builds software bots that automate repetitive, rule-based work such as data entry, invoice processing and report generation. This hour, “Building an RPA portfolio”, is where that becomes concrete. If you skip it, later talk about Professional RPA development turns into words you cannot cash.

items: RPA with UiPath, expert level
